newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Rescuers search Russian blast site as PM flies in.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers search Russian blast site as PM flies in.

text.p: Rescue workers on Sunday frantically sifted through rubble looking for survivors of a blast, feared to be the work of saboteurs, that wrecked a block of flats housing military personnel.
The death toll from the explosion, which happened early on Saturday in Russia's southern republic of Dagestan, had reached 24, including nine children, by Sunday afternoon, a local official said.
Other Russian news reports earlier put the death toll at up to 32. Tass said a third of the Caspian region's border guards may have been wiped out in the explosion.
A spokesman for Dagestani authorities said 24 dead and eight injured people had been pulled from the ruins of the eight- storey building and 35 were still assumed to be in the rubble.
"Although the work was scheduled to be finished today and is quite active, the end is not yet in sight and the rescuers will continue working throughout the night," he said by telephone.
"We expect to get into the basement of the building tonight, which will shed some light on the cause of the blast," said a spokesman for the local emergencies ministry department.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin flew to this small port by the Caspian Sea on Sunday after promising a thorough investigation into the disaster.
The blast occurred while residents, mostly families of border guards and airforce officers, were sleeping.
"I thought I was having a bad dream. Everything began falling on me and then a man called Akhmed rescued me," 12-year-old Roxana told Reuters at a local hospital where many of the injured were taken.
Other girls in her ward were anxious to find out whether their families and friends were still alive.

Rescue workers, including teams flown in from Moscow, used cranes, sniffer dogs and electric drills in their hunt for survivors. Russian television said that by Sunday afternoon they were dragging out mostly dead bodies.
Regional authorities have declared Sunday and Monday official days of mourning in Dagestan, which borders the breakaway Russian republic of Chechnya.
Some officials said there might be a link between the explosion and Chechnya, where an uneasy peace is holding after a 21-month bloody conflict between Russian forces and separatists.
Local residents shared their suspicions.
"Those bloody Chechens are responsible for this," one woman told Chernomyrdin as he toured the scene of the disaster.
"Why do we bring up our boys so that the state can then send them off to war where they get killed?" she said. The Chechen war was deeply unpopular in Russia.

Chechen rebel leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, whose aide worked out a new draft agreement with Moscow on Saturday, on Sunday denied the separatists were involved in the blast, which he said was aimed at wrecking the peace process.

Russia's Interior Ministry said it had not ruled out the possibility of a terrorist action, and Tass quoted official sources as saying it might be a gangland revenge attack linked to a regional crackdown on arms and caviar smuggling.

Gangland violence has become a commonplace in post-communist Russia. Last weekend 14 people died in a bomb blast at a Moscow cemetery apparently triggered by a feud between warring factions of an Afghan war veterans' charity with big business links.

Border guards dismissed the possibility of a gas explosion because they said the building was not connected to gas mains. Agencies reported signs that TNT explosive had been detonated in the building.

President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery, has sent his condolences to relatives of the dead and the government has set up a commission under a deputy prime minister, Oleg Lobov, to investigate the causes of the blast.
